title: Let-Me-In: (Still) Employing In-pointer Bounds Metadata for Fine-grained GPU Memory Safety
problem: GPU programs written in C/C++ inherit memory safety vulnerabilities such as out-of-bounds accesses. The heterogeneous GPU memory hierarchy (heap, local memory, thousands of concurrent threads) makes it difficult to enforce fine-grained bounds checking with low overhead.
motivation: As GPUs are deployed in safety-critical systems (autonomous driving, medical diagnostics), memory corruption bugs pose serious reliability and security risks, and existing GPU memory safety schemes impose prohibitive metadata storage or performance costs.
method: The system aligns GPU memory to power-of-two boundaries (allocations at multiples of 2) and performs static analysis—inspecting the code before it runs—to mark instructions that perform pointer arithmetic (operations that calculate new memory addresses). Instead of storing bounds information in separate tables, it encodes the size and base address of each allocated block directly into the unused upper bits of the 64-bit addresses that GPUs use. Before each memory access executes, hardware logic validates it against the bounds encoded in the pointer itself, all with minimal added latency even when thousands of operations run concurrently.
key_novelty: The core idea is storing each object's bounds information entirely in the unused upper bits of GPU pointers—using power-of-two alignment and static marking of which operations change memory addresses—instead of keeping separate bounds tables.
contributions: Fine-grained GPU memory safety mechanism (LMI) covering heap and local memory with negligible hardware overhead
Power-of-two allocation alignment strategy that enables in-pointer metadata encoding on GPUs
Static analysis pass that identifies and marks pointer arithmetic instructions to enable runtime bounds derivation
Evaluation demonstrating near-zero performance and hardware cost overhead compared to prior GPU memory safety proposals

metrics.other: negligible performance overhead vs baseline GPU execution

limitations: Coverage is limited to heap and local memory; global/shared GPU memory safety and complex pointer aliasing patterns may not be fully addressed.
primary_theme: fine-grained GPU memory safety via in-pointer metadata
